At 10% research progress, prioritize **absolute-event-recency-weighted BPR-max** within corrected GRU4Rec. Benefits remain unmeasured; retain window-position weighting as a distinct control.

**Insights from the starting point.** (1) Electronics has 22.31% small sampled margins and 9.01% negative-over-positive rankings, motivating discrimination experiments without establishing validation failure causes. (2) Users report stale interests displacing current preferences. Weighting targets by their distance from the latest training event directly emphasizes recent supervision, but does not make the recurrent state forget old inputs. (3) Users distinguish specific matches from broad affinity. Competitive negatives may challenge broad matches, but cannot establish purpose, ownership duplication, or compatibility.

**Insights from related work.** (1) [GRU4Rec](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf) supplies BPR-max and negative-score regularization; they require separate controls. (2) [Sampling evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) is dataset-dependent, supporting uniform sampling as a control. (3) [MTAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) concerns recurrent retention; [RSS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) concerns supervision selection. Neither establishes that window-end weighting removes stale preferences.

**Framework.** Separate discrimination, target exposure, and state retention. Window position measures available context; absolute event age measures training-history recency; timestamp age measures elapsed time. These are distinct mechanisms.

**Candidate assessment.** Scores are originality/potential/user alignment/model alignment/difficulty; higher difficulty means harder implementation. Each cell states a positive and a limitation.

| Idea | Scores | Positive and negative assessment |
|---|---|---|
| A: absolute-recency BPR-max | 3/6/5/8/4 | O: diagnosis-led combination, established parts; P: reusable objective, uncertain transfer; U: targets stale and broad matches, weak intent proxy; M: targets weak margins, possible score inflation; D: localized loss, requires original target indices. |
| B: gap-conditioned GRU retention | 5/7/8/6/6 | O: content-conditioned forgetting, temporal precedents; P: models drift, gaps may mislead; U: targets stale and context-mismatched choices, gaps do not reveal intent; M: indirect separation benefit; D: compact gate, timestamp integration required. |
| C: jointly trained title encoder | 4/7/7/6/7 | O: semantic/recurrent combination, established ingredients; P: finer matching, sparse supervision; U: specificity and compatibility cues, incomplete descriptions; M: richer features, possible increased alignment; D: one checkpoint, vocabulary integration required. |

**Selected algorithm A.** Use 16 total uniform negatives per transition, temperature 1, event half-life 10, and per-user-normalized weights. Preserve the proposed 0.01 negative-score penalty as a separate experimental arm. Target stale-interest dominance and broad competitors, plus weak Electronics margins; improvements in these user failures require fresh qualitative evidence.

Prespecify a 2×2 comparison: mean pairwise BPR versus BPR-max, crossed with uniform versus absolute-event weighting, all using 16 negatives and zero score penalty. Retain the supplied baseline as context; separately test penalty 0.01, window weighting, and negative count only if budget permits. Select by pinned macro validation HR@10. Report all trials, runtime, exposures, and conditional paired bootstrap contrasts; validation reuse still creates selection optimism. Preserve four routes, seeds, limits, diagnostics, final-nonpadding readout, and one matching checkpoint per category.

idea.description: Absolute-event-recency-weighted BPR-max for the supplied corrected GRU4Rec, with exactly one independently trained model per category. Separate ranking objective, target weighting, negative count, and negative-score regularization through prespecified comparisons. Keep window-position weighting as an explicitly different control.
idea.motivation: The selected idea explicitly targets two user-facing failures: older interests displacing recent preferences, and broadly related candidates competing with specific matches. Absolute-event weighting emphasizes supervision near each user's latest observed training event; BPR-max emphasizes competitive sampled candidates. These are indirect mechanisms: neither identifies current purpose, functional duplication, compatibility, or confirmed dislike. The model-facing target is weak sampled separation, especially Electronics' 0.0427 lower-decile margin, 22.31% small-margin rate, and 9.01% negative-over-positive rate. Industrial_and_Scientific is the next priority. CDs_and_Vinyl's strong training margins do not establish validation quality. Mean embedding alignment is not proof of collapse, and this loss does not directly remedy anisotropy.
idea.implementation_notes:
Preserve the supplied GRU architecture, score activation, recurrent state reset/carry policy, window length, optimizer, initialization, and inference scoring. Preserve preprocessing seed 0, training seed 42, supplied splits, all four category routes, single-GPU execution, at most 200 epochs and 200 batches per epoch, and the shared 43,200 GPU-second budget. DATA_DIR remains os.environ['GAGC_DATA_DIR']; save artifacts beneath the trial directory. Do not inspect other trials, hidden test files, or held-out positives for sampling exclusions.

The baseline source is unavailable in this prompt; the code below is an integration-ready objective, not a complete replacement train.py. Each sampled target must carry its original zero-based index k in that user's training history of length T_u. Its absolute event age is T_u - 1 - k, regardless of sampled-window position. This uses only training histories. Timestamp-age weighting would require separately validated timestamp units and references; it is not implemented here. If the adapter cannot supply original indices, implement the window control and label it accurately rather than claiming absolute recency.

Use 16 TOTAL negative columns per valid transition, without additional minibatch negatives. Draw uniformly with replacement from real item IDs excluding the user's complete training-history items and the current training target. Keep duplicate negative IDs as separate columns, report duplicate rates and unique counts, and mask transitions with no eligible negative. This is a deliberate departure from official GRU4Rec sampling, which combines additional popularity-tempered draws with minibatch targets and generally retains collisions. Apply the proposed rejection policy identically across controlled arms; do not call it verified false-negative detection. An eligible unseen item can still be relevant.

For the primary 2×2 experiment, cross mean pairwise BPR/BPR-max with uniform/absolute-event weighting, fixing K=16, temperature=1 and score_reg=0. Use half_life=10 events for weighted arms. Preserve the original proposal's score_reg=0.01 as a separately identified extension, not part of the isolated loss contrast. The supplied cold start is an additional contextual baseline if its sampling differs. If budget remains, separately compare K=1 versus K=16, score_reg=0 versus 0.01, and window versus absolute recency on identical windows. With K=1 and score_reg=0, both objective implementations must coincide. Do not expand every suggested control into a full factorial search.

Use the supplied baseline optimizer settings rather than inventing replacements. Generate identical training windows and negatives across controlled arms using a dedicated deterministic sampling stream seeded 42, separate from model/dropout randomness. Initialize each category identically across arms. Equalize update counts, loss scale, checkpoint evaluation schedule and selection rule, and disclose runtime because equal update counts have unequal cost. Keep sequences at their supplied sampling frequency. The implementation normalizes within each sampled sequence, then averages sequences; it is per-user normalization only when the sampler supplies one window per selected user. Otherwise describe it as per-window normalization, or aggregate all selected windows for a user before normalization. Report effective exposure by original event age, window position and history length; normalization alone does not guarantee equal influence across users.

BPR-max is the negative logarithm of a softmax-weighted probability sum. Keep gradients through negative weights in both ranking and score-penalty terms. The squared-negative-score penalty is distinct from optimizer weight decay. Stable logsumexp avoids adding a numerically arbitrary epsilon. Monitor score norms and held-fixed sampled margins to distinguish separation from score inflation. Retain the exact diagnostic definitions: valid input, positive and negative IDs must all be nonzero. Use comparable diagnostic samples across arms; altered optimization-negative counts must not silently alter reported diagnostic comparisons.

Retain DiagnosisProbe(view, device), run_full_diagnosis(train_loader) returning metrics and metric_definitions, and diagnosis_interpreter_prompt(raw_diagnosis). Preserve view.model, item_emb, log2feats(sequence), predict_score(features, items), user_train, meta_data and review_data interfaces. The required diagnostic loader remains (None, sequence, positive, negative), each tensor B×L; original target ages belong in the training sampler's separate path rather than replacing that interface. Use only public histories, titles, descriptions and timestamps; unavailable ratings, categories, prices, stores, review text and simulator traits remain unavailable.

Because the architecture is unchanged, no new inference features are required. Keep the predictor writer synchronized with the actual architecture and checkpoint configuration. For left-padded histories, gather the final nonpadding position using the maximum nonzero index, never count-1, and preserve baseline handling of empty histories. Each category loads exactly one checkpoint; ablation arms are alternative experiments and are never fused or averaged.

Prespecify checkpoint selection before execution: use the baseline validation cadence and a common four-category evaluation schedule; select each arm's category checkpoints from one common evaluation point maximizing macro validation HR@10, breaking ties by earliest point. Select the final arm by that same pinned metric and disclose all evaluated points and trials. Do not introduce a surrogate metric or modify the host evaluator. If the host exposes per-user validation hit indicators, retain them on identical users/candidates. Resample 200 users within each category with replacement for 10,000 paired bootstrap replicates using a separate analysis RNG seed 42 and common draws across arms. Compute equally weighted macro HR and percentile 95% intervals. Prespecify loss, weighting and interaction contrasts; use simultaneous intervals for the declared comparison family. These intervals condition on fitted seed-42 models and fixed candidates; they do not cover training, category or candidate-sampling variability, and winner-only intervals do not remove adaptive selection bias. If per-user indicators are unavailable, omit these intervals rather than reconstructing them from aggregate HR. One changed hit changes macro HR by 0.00125. Sampled HR need not preserve full-catalog rankings.

Validate the two user-facing hypotheses through the existing twenty-user full-catalog unseen-item diagnosis: track stale-interest objections and specific-current-intent endorsements versus broad-interest endorsements. Keep duplication, compatibility, deferred interest and unidentified content as separate observed judgments. Do not claim these improve from margins or HR alone. Final held-out assessment remains the host's separate evaluation step.
idea.pseudocode:
import math
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def ranking_objective(pos_logits, neg_logits, valid, target_age=None,
                      objective='bpr_max', half_life=10.0,
                      temperature=1.0, score_reg=0.0):
    """pos [B,L], neg [B,L,K], valid [B,L].
    target_age=None gives uniform weighting. Otherwise age [B,L]
    is original training-event distance, NOT sampled-window distance.
    Reduction averages normalized sampled sequences; user weighting
    additionally depends on the sampler.
    """
    if objective not in ('bpr', 'bpr_max'):
        raise ValueError('Unknown objective')
    if temperature <= 0 or half_life <= 0 or score_reg < 0:
        raise ValueError('Invalid hyperparameters')
    if neg_logits.shape[-1] == 0:
        raise ValueError('At least one eligible negative is required')
    valid = valid.bool()
    rows, cols = valid.nonzero(as_tuple=True)
    if rows.numel() == 0:
        return pos_logits[valid].sum() * 0.0

    p = pos_logits[rows, cols].float()
    n = neg_logits[rows, cols].float()
    delta = p[:, None] - n
    if objective == 'bpr_max':
        log_q = F.log_softmax(n / temperature, dim=-1)
        ranking = -torch.logsumexp(
            log_q + F.logsigmoid(delta), dim=-1)
        penalty = score_reg * (log_q.exp() * n.square()).sum(-1)
    else:
        if score_reg != 0:
            raise ValueError('Primary pairwise control uses zero penalty')
        ranking = -F.logsigmoid(delta).mean(-1)
        penalty = torch.zeros_like(ranking)

    if target_age is None:
        log_weight = torch.zeros_like(p)
    else:
        age = target_age[rows, cols].float()
        if not torch.isfinite(age).all() or (age < 0).any():
            raise ValueError('Valid target ages must be finite and nonnegative')
        log_weight = -math.log(2.0) * age / half_life

    # Subtract each row maximum to avoid underflow; normalization
    # is mathematically unchanged.
    batch_size = pos_logits.shape[0]
    row_max = torch.full((batch_size,), -torch.inf, device=p.device)
    row_max.scatter_reduce_(0, rows, log_weight,
                            reduce='amax', include_self=True)
    weight = torch.exp(log_weight - row_max[rows])
    denom = torch.zeros(batch_size, device=p.device)
    denom.scatter_add_(0, rows, weight)
    per_sequence = torch.zeros_like(denom)
    per_sequence.scatter_add_(
        0, rows, weight * (ranking + penalty) / denom[rows])
    return per_sequence[denom > 0].mean()


# Training adapter for each required category:
# 1. Load supplied fixed splits; initialize corrected GRU with seed 42.
# 2. Sample identical windows across controlled arms, retaining original
#    training target index k and user training-history length T_u.
# 3. Set absolute_age = T_u - 1 - k at every valid target position.
# 4. Draw K=16 TOTAL uniform negatives with replacement, rejecting
#    padding and known training-history items; retain duplicate columns.
# 5. valid requires nonzero sequence/positive IDs and eligible negatives.
# 6. Obtain logits through the unchanged GRU scoring interfaces.
# 7. Cross objective in {bpr, bpr_max} with ages in {None, absolute_age};
#    use score_reg=0, temperature=1, half_life=10 for the primary factorial.
# 8. Preserve all baseline training settings and common validation cadence.
# 9. If budget permits, test score_reg=0.01, window ages, and K separately.
#    Window age = number of valid targets after this position in its window.
# 10. Verify K=1, score_reg=0 objective equality; check padding, exclusions,
#     finite extreme-age losses and non-detached BPR-max weight gradients.
# 11. Diagnose using unchanged BxL probe batches and common sampled negatives.
# 12. Select by host macro validation HR@10; disclose all trials/checkpoints.
# 13. Export exactly one selected checkpoint per category with matching writer.
#     Never fuse arms. Final readout uses maximum nonzero sequence index.

# Prespecified paired contrasts on common evaluation users/candidates:
# A = mean BPR, uniform; B = BPR-max, uniform
# C = mean BPR, absolute recency; D = BPR-max, absolute recency
# loss effect = ((B-A) + (D-C)) / 2
# weighting effect = ((C-A) + (D-B)) / 2
# interaction = D-C-B+A
# Bootstrap users independently within category, paired across arms;
# average four category HR values equally. Retain conditional interpretation.

originality.positive: Distinguishes absolute training-event recency from sampled-window position and combines that supervision policy with a diagnosis-motivated competitive GRU loss.
originality.negative: BPR-max, exponential recency weighting, and factorial ablations are established techniques; the proposal is a controlled empirical hypothesis rather than a new model class.

future_potential.positive: A small objective change can establish whether target exposure or discrimination merits further investment before adding temporal gates or jointly trained text features.
future_potential.negative: No supplied experiment demonstrates improved validation HR@10 or immediate-choice alignment; recency can amplify transient behavior and harder negatives can suppress relevant unseen items.

code_difficulty.positive: The recurrent backbone, inference inputs, and checkpoint architecture remain unchanged, and the objective is compact.
code_difficulty.negative: Original target-index tracking, controlled sampling streams, normalization semantics, negative exclusions, budgeted comparisons, and predictor/diagnostic consistency require integration beyond a loss replacement.

related_work.title: Recurrent Neural Networks with Top-k Gains for Session-based Recommendations
contributions: Introduces competitive ranking objectives including BPR-max and negative-score regularization for recurrent recommendation.
Supports the weighted probability-sum objective rather than a weighted sum of pairwise log-losses.
limitations: Does not establish gains for these Amazon splits or absolute-event recency weighting.
Official sampling differs from the proposed history-excluding uniform pool, so implementation provenance and controlled comparisons must be explicit.

related_work.title: Official GRU4Rec PyTorch implementation
contributions: Provides concrete BPR-max loss and sampling implementations.
Clarifies additional sampled negatives versus minibatch negatives, retained duplicate columns, and collision behavior.
limitations: Copying its sampling terminology without reproducing its candidate construction would make negative-count comparisons misleading.
It does not implement the proposed absolute-event weighting control.

related_work.title: Sequential recommendation negative-sampling study supplied in the search results
contributions: Compares sampling strategies and reports variation across datasets and item popularity.
limitations: Provides no universal guarantee that more competitive negatives improve ranking or represent genuine dislikes.

related_work.title: MTAM
contributions: Uses temporal gating and recurrent modeling to capture changing sequential preferences.
limitations: Recurrent retention differs from target-loss weighting and requires architecture and timestamp integration.
Does not establish that positional weighting or hard resets resolve preference drift here.

related_work.title: Petrov and Macdonald RSS study
contributions: Studies supervision selection and exponential target sampling with fixed recommendation architectures, including GRU4Rec.
limitations: RSS removes sampled targets and changes the prediction task, so it does not isolate weighted next-item losses.

related_work.title: Recency Dropout
contributions: Investigates recurrent forgetting through simulations and Jacobian analysis.
limitations: Input sensitivity and recurrent forgetting are distinct from assigning larger weights to recent prediction targets.

related_work.title: On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation
contributions: Examines limitations of recommendation evaluation using sampled candidates.
limitations: Does not justify changing the pinned benchmark; its relevance is to limiting claims about full-catalog ranking.

related_work.title: On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation
contributions: Explains selection optimism caused by optimizing and repeatedly reusing validation estimates.
limitations: Does not provide an automatic correction for adaptive validation reuse; ordinary bootstrap intervals and multiplicity adjustment do not replace independent evaluation.
